title: Zephyr devicetree for beginners: describing hardware so drivers can find it
summary: How Zephyr uses devicetree nodes, properties, overlays and bindings to tell drivers where a peripheral lives and which pins it uses, all resolved at build time into C macros.

title: Your first time as a technical lead: planning, unblocking and reviewing
summary: A new technical lead's job shifts from doing the work to making the team's work succeed. How to break work down, keep people unblocked, review well, and still keep your own engineering skills sharp.

title: Your first cocotb testbench: clock, reset, drive and check a counter
summary: Build a complete self-checking cocotb testbench in Python for a 4-bit counter, and learn what await, the clock task, reset and ReadOnly actually do in simulation time.

title: Your first circuit in Xschem and ngspice: an inverter from schematic to transient plot
summary: Draw a CMOS inverter in Xschem with sky130 transistors, generate a SPICE netlist, simulate it in ngspice and measure its delay. Each step explains what the tool is doing so you can debug it yourself.

title: X in RTL simulation: how unknowns hide bugs and how to flush them out
summary: Why if and case statements swallow X values in RTL simulation, how that hides missing resets, and how assertions, coding style and randomised initial values make uninitialised state visible.

title: Writing your first SDC: clocks, I/O delays and false paths
summary: Timing tools only check what your constraints describe. Build a minimum SDC for a block, line by line, and learn the over-constraints and missing constraints that hide real failing paths.

title: Writing the requirements for a BLDC motor controller, from fans to e-mobility
summary: How to capture speed range, efficiency, protection, acoustic noise, EMC and certification needs for a BLDC motor controller as testable requirements, and how they change from a ceiling fan to a vehicle.

title: Writing reusable Verilog with parameters and generate blocks
summary: Width parameters, localparam, generate loops and generate-if let one module serve many sizes. Learn the patterns and the elaboration errors beginners hit most often, with fixes.

title: Writing requirements that can be tested: shall, measurable, one thing each
summary: How to turn a wish like "long battery life" into a requirement with a number, a unit, a condition and an agreed test, so that everyone can tell whether the product passes.

title: Writing int8 inference for one dense layer in plain C
summary: A complete int8 dense layer in portable C - integer multiply-accumulate, 32-bit accumulators, requantization with a fixed-point multiplier and shift - and a numpy-generated test that proves it bit-exact.

title: Writing an interrupt-safe ring buffer for UART receive
summary: A UART interrupt fills a buffer and the main loop empties it. With one writer per index, free-running counters and the right memory ordering, you need no lock and lose no bytes.

title: Writing a weekly status update that managers and peers can scan
summary: A good weekly status update fits in a few lines, done, next, blocked and risks, each backed by a link to evidence rather than adjectives. Here is the format, a worked example and the mistakes to avoid.

title: Writing a verification plan that someone can actually check against
summary: Turn a specification into numbered plan items, each with a stimulus, a check and a coverage goal, so that anyone can trace a requirement to the test that proves it.

title: Writing a small device driver: the layers between a register and an API
summary: Build an I2C sensor driver in four layers: a register map, a replaceable bus interface, a checked initialisation sequence and an interrupt-backed API with clear units that you can test on a laptop.

title: Writing a little RISC-V assembly to understand what your C compiles to
summary: Read compiler output for a loop and a function call with the RISC-V calling convention in hand. Learn which register holds what, why the stack frame looks the way it does, and how to check your reading.

title: Writing a blameless postmortem after a failed lab or project
summary: How to write a postmortem after a project goes wrong: a factual timeline, contributing causes found with "why" questions, what went well, and concrete actions with owners, all without blaming people.

title: Writing a README that explains your project in two minutes
summary: A README should answer five questions in order, what it is, why it matters, how to run it, what the results are and where it stops, so a stranger understands your project in two minutes.

title: Working in a capstone team: roles, milestones and disagreements
summary: How a small capstone team avoids the usual failures: agree interfaces and owners in week one, track milestones by what is tested, and settle technical disagreements with data instead of volume.

title: Wireless products in India: the approvals to plan for before launch
summary: Why products with radios need equipment and frequency approvals, how licence-exempt bands, power limits and antenna choices shape the design, and why the approval plan belongs in the first design review.

title: Will the model fit? Estimating flash and RAM for TinyML
summary: Weights go in flash, activations go in RAM, and the tensor arena holds the live ones. A worked estimate for a small audio network shows how to size both before you write any firmware.

title: Will every task meet its deadline? Response-time analysis worked by hand
summary: The utilisation bound only says yes or don't know. Response-time analysis gives each task's exact worst case under fixed-priority preemption: the equation, a worked example and what real systems add.

title: Why owning design IP matters for an electronics ecosystem
summary: The difference between assembling electronic products and owning their designs, how owning the design changes who controls cost, features and supply, and what it means for the skills engineers build.

title: Why low-cost water quality sensing matters, and what makes it hard
summary: Why continuous water quality monitoring is useful, and why sensor drift, fouling, calibration and maintenance, not the electronics, are the real obstacles, with a simulation of drift and recalibration.

title: Why hold violations are worse than setup violations, and how tools fix them
summary: A setup failure on silicon can be slowed away; a hold failure cannot, because the clock period is not in the hold equation. See why, and what buffer insertion to fix hold costs in area and power.

title: Why an I2C bus gets stuck low, and how firmware recovers it
summary: If the controller resets in the middle of a read, a target can hold SDA low forever, waiting for clocks that never come. Clocking out the rest of the byte and sending a STOP releases the bus.

title: Why a two-flop synchronizer works, and when it doesn't
summary: A two-flop synchronizer buys a metastable flip-flop one full clock period to settle. Here is the MTBF reasoning behind it, and the buses, pulses and fast-to-slow cases it cannot fix.

title: Why RISC-V scrambles its immediate bits
summary: Branch and jump offsets in RISC-V look shuffled. Count the multiplexer inputs in the immediate generator and you see why: the shuffle keeps each bit in one place across formats and saves logic.

title: Why BLDC motors are spreading in fans and appliances, and the chip inside
summary: How a brushless DC motor uses electronic commutation instead of an induction motor's slip and how that saves energy, with a worked comparison and a walk through what the controller chip actually does.

title: Why 100% code coverage does not mean the design is verified
summary: Line, branch, toggle and FSM coverage show which parts of the RTL were exercised. They cannot show wrong conditions that were never tested at the boundary, unchecked outputs, or features nobody wrote.

title: Which corners to sign off: process, voltage and temperature for digital timing
summary: Setup is signed off where cells are slowest and hold where they are fastest. Learn which process, voltage and temperature combinations that means, and how on-chip variation derates tighten every check.

title: Where dynamic power goes: activity, capacitance, voltage and frequency
summary: Dynamic power is activity times capacitance times voltage squared times frequency. Apply the equation to a small RTL block and see which of the four terms an RTL designer can actually change.

title: Where accidental latches come from, and how to read the synthesis warning
summary: A combinational block that does not assign every output on every path makes synthesis infer a latch. Learn to spot the cause, read the warning, and prevent it with defaults and always_comb.

title: When to ask for help, and how to ask so you get a useful answer
summary: Asking for help is a skill. Time-box your own attempt, then ask with context, what you tried and a minimal example, so a busy senior can answer in minutes instead of starting from zero.

title: When gate-level simulation is still worth running
summary: Equivalence checking and static timing cover most of what gate-level simulation once did. What remains: reset and initialisation bugs, X behaviour, constraint mistakes and test or power modes.

title: What volatile really does in embedded C, and what it does not
summary: volatile tells the compiler that every read and write of a variable matters, so hardware registers and ISR flags work. It does not make an access atomic or ordered, and it is not a lock.

title: What simulation cannot tell you about clock domain crossings
summary: RTL simulation never goes metastable and resolves every synchronizer in a fixed number of cycles, so it hides real CDC bugs. Structural checks, randomised synchronizer delay and targeted assertions fill the gap.

title: What logic synthesis actually does to your RTL
summary: Synthesis elaborates your RTL, optimises it as generic logic, then maps it onto real library cells. Here is what happens at each stage and how to read the cell-count report it leaves behind.

title: What happens in an assembly and test facility: from wafer to packaged, tested part
summary: The steps a finished wafer goes through to become a packaged, tested chip, in order, from wafer probing and dicing to die attach, bonding, moulding, final test and burn-in, and what each step guards against.

title: What happens before main(): startup code on a microcontroller
summary: Between reset and the first line of main() a few dozen instructions set the stack pointer, copy initialised globals into RAM and zero the rest. Here is each step on a RISC-V microcontroller, and why C needs it.

title: What an instruction set promises, and what it leaves to the hardware
summary: An instruction set is a contract. Learn exactly what it guarantees to software, what it deliberately leaves open, and why that freedom lets one binary run on very different cores.

title: What a low-cost vision sensor can classify on-chip
summary: Resolution, memory and compute set hard limits on an always-on camera node. Working through pixels on target, frame buffers and MACs per frame shows which vision tasks fit and which do not.

title: What a drone flight-controller SoC needs: latency, sensor interfaces and safety
summary: A flight controller is a hard real-time system with many serial and PWM interfaces and no tolerance for hangs. Derive its SoC requirements from a control-loop latency budget, the sensor list and the fail-safes.

title: What NavIC is, and what it takes to build a receiver for it
summary: NavIC is India's regional satellite navigation system. This article explains how it differs from global systems, how any satellite receiver finds its position, and what a NavIC receiver chip has to do.

title: What BIS registration and certification mean for an electronics product
summary: What India's national standards body does, how product registration and certification work in outline, what an engineer must prepare for them, and why you must check the current product lists yourself.

title: Weight-stationary, output-stationary and row-stationary dataflows compared
summary: An accelerator dataflow is named for the data that stays put in each processing element. Counting buffer accesses for one matrix multiply shows how that choice, and the loop order behind it, sets traffic and energy.

title: Virtual memory and the TLB: translating addresses without slowing down
summary: A RISC-V Sv32 page walk worked step by step, why every access cannot afford it, and the TLB choices that hide it (reach, superpages, ASIDs, fences, the VIPT limit).

title: Verifying battery-protection logic: over-voltage, under-voltage and fault latching
summary: Assertions and directed corner tests for a battery protection block, covering thresholds, debounce, latched faults and safe reset states, where a single missed case can leave a cell unprotected.

title: Verifying an ML accelerator against a numpy golden model
summary: An ML accelerator is verified like any datapath, against a bit-exact integer reference. Writing that numpy golden model, choosing random and corner tensors, and comparing layer by layer to localise bugs.

title: Verifying a UART end to end: framing, baud error and coverage closure
summary: Check every field of a UART frame, work out how much baud mismatch a receiver must tolerate and test it with a fractional-rate driver, then close coverage on parity, framing and glitch errors.

title: Verifying a RISC-V core against a reference model in lockstep
summary: Compare a core's architectural state with an instruction set simulator after every retired instruction, and handle the hard parts - traps, interrupts, counters and device reads - without false mismatches.

title: Verification and validation: building the right product vs building it right
summary: Verification checks that the product meets its requirements; validation checks that it meets the user's real need. Examples of each, the V-model that links them, and how a product can pass one and fail the other.

title: Using a watchdog properly: what to kick, where, and when not to
summary: A watchdog only helps if it is refreshed when the whole system is healthy. How to collect check-ins from every task, size the timeout, use a windowed watchdog, and record why the last reset happened.

title: Using NavIC alongside other satellite systems in one receiver
summary: Why multi-constellation receivers track more satellites, how they cope with different signal structures and bands, and how one extra unknown per system absorbs the offset between their time references.

title: Using AI tools responsibly in engineering: by hand first, then check
summary: Do a task yourself first so you can judge what an AI assistant gives you, then verify generated code with the same tests, lint and review you would apply to any other code. Here is why, and how.

title: Using AI to write testbench code without trusting it blindly
summary: Write the first test by hand, then let an AI assistant draft more, and review every generated check against the spec. A worked review shows the flaws that make generated tests pass while checking nothing.

title: Unit testing firmware on your laptop: separating logic from hardware
summary: Most firmware bugs are in ordinary logic, not in register writes. Split the two, swap registers for a fake array on the host, and a plain gcc build can test your code in seconds with sanitizers switched on.

title: UVM in one diagram: sequences, drivers, monitors and the agent
summary: One picture of a UVM testbench, from test to pins, with what each component owns, how transactions flow between them, and why splitting the work this way lets the same pieces be reused.

title: UART, SPI or I2C: choosing a serial bus for a sensor
summary: A practical comparison of UART, SPI and I2C for connecting sensors to a microcontroller, covering pin count, bandwidth worked out per sample, addressing, cable length and how each bus tells you something went wrong.

title: Two's complement from the hardware side: why one adder does signed and unsigned
summary: The same binary adder adds signed and unsigned numbers; only the interpretation and the overflow check differ. Learn the overflow rules, sign extension and the Verilog signed traps.

title: Treating models like firmware: versioning, tests and CI for edge AI
summary: A deployed model is part of the firmware image and deserves the same discipline - pinned and hashed model files, regression tests on frozen held-out data, bit-exact checks of the device code, and budgets enforced in CI.

title: Traceability from requirement to test: why it saves projects
summary: Linking every requirement up to a need and down to design items and tests makes gaps and the impact of changes visible. A small Python script shows how to find both.

title: Timing closure when the last few paths will not close
summary: When a handful of paths stay negative after every optimisation run, more tool effort rarely helps. A decision order for checking constraints, path structure, floorplan and RTL before touching tool knobs.

title: Timers in practice: PWM output, input capture and the prescaler arithmetic
summary: How a hardware timer turns a clock into PWM and pulse measurements, how to pick prescaler and period values for a target frequency and resolution, and how to measure a pulse that spans a counter wrap.

title: Three open PDKs and what each is good for
summary: sky130, gf180 and IHP SG13G2 are open process design kits you can use for real chips. Compare them by process type, voltages, metal stack and typical uses, and learn how to pick one for a project.

title: Thermal design basics: junction temperature and heat paths
summary: How to estimate a part's junction temperature from its power and the thermal resistances between die and air, why copper area and airflow change the answer, and how to check the result against the part's limits.

title: Thermal and flicker noise in analog front ends
summary: Resistors and transistors add random noise that sets the smallest signal a front end can see. Learn where thermal and flicker noise come from, how to refer noise to the input, and how to size a stage for low noise.

title: The valid/ready handshake: the rules that keep pipelines from losing data
summary: A transfer happens on a clock edge where valid and ready are both high. Learn the rules that follow from that, why valid must never wait for ready, and how backpressure ripples back through pipeline stages.

title: The tape-out checklist: what to confirm before you send GDS
summary: Once GDS leaves your hands, nothing can be changed. Work through a tape-out checklist covering physical checks, timing at every corner, precheck, documentation and a bring-up plan, with a small script to gate a run.

title: The metering front end of a smart energy meter: shunts, current transformers and simultaneous sampling
summary: An energy meter multiplies voltage by current thousands of times a second. Learn how shunts, current transformers and dividers sense them, why a few microseconds of skew ruins accuracy, and how meters are calibrated.

title: The load-use hazard: why one bubble remains even with forwarding
summary: A load's data arrives at the end of the memory stage, one cycle too late to forward into the next instruction's ALU. Learn why, how the pipeline detects it and stalls, and how compilers hide the bubble.

title: The iron law of performance: instructions, CPI and clock period
summary: Execution time is instruction count times cycles per instruction times clock period. Learn where each factor comes from, compute CPI from an instruction mix, and see how compilers, caches and pipelines move each one.

title: The instrumentation amplifier: measuring tiny differences on large common-mode signals
summary: The three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier gives high input impedance, gain set by one resistor and strong common-mode rejection. Learn how each stage works and why resistor matching sets the rejection.

title: The hardware product lifecycle from concept to end-of-life
summary: The stages a hardware product passes through, from concept and prototypes through engineering, design and production validation builds to mass production, support and planned end-of-life, and what each gate decides.

title: The first day with your chip back from the fab: a bring-up plan
summary: Bring-up goes in a fixed order so that one fault cannot hide another or destroy the part. Learn a staged plan: current-limited power-up, clocks and reset, JTAG and scan, then functions, with everything recorded.

title: The electronics inside e-rickshaw battery systems, and where a BMS chip fits
summary: How a small traction battery pack is built from cells, and how its battery management system measures, protects, balances and reports, with a worked balancing calculation and what a dedicated chip could integrate.

title: The differential pair: why analog designers love it
summary: Two matched transistors and a tail current amplify the difference between two inputs and ignore what they share. Learn how the pair steers current, its gain, its common-mode rejection, and its role in op-amps.

title: The common-source amplifier: gain, headroom and the gm-ro trade-off
summary: The common-source stage is the workhorse gain stage of CMOS analog design. Work out its small-signal gain, its output swing limits, and why longer transistors buy gain at the cost of speed.

title: The MOSFET in three regions: an intuition-first guide
summary: A MOSFET is off, behaves like a resistor, or behaves like a current source, depending on two voltages. Build the picture with water flow first, then the square-law equations and a worked example.

title: The M and C extensions: what multiply and compressed instructions cost in hardware
summary: Adding M means choosing a multiplier and divider; adding C means a decompressor and a fetch unit that handles 16-bit alignment. What each costs, what it buys, and how to measure the trade for your product.

title: The Linux shell skills every chip and firmware engineer uses
summary: Chip and firmware tools run from the Linux shell. Learn the daily skills that matter, navigating, searching logs, pipes, small scripts and environment variables, with examples from real tool flows.

title: Testing an APB register block with pyuvm, from sequence to scoreboard
summary: A walk-through of a pyuvm environment for a four-register APB slave, with a spec-derived register model, a wait-state-aware driver, reset-value checks and a scoreboard that predicts side effects.

title: Telling sensor drift from real events in water quality data
summary: A water quality reading can change because the water changed or because the sensor did. Moving statistics, reference checks and a few explainable rules separate slow drift from genuine events.

title: Technical writing for engineers: lead with the conclusion
summary: Put the answer in the first sentence, follow it with only the evidence the reader needs to trust it, and cut the rest. A method for emails, reports and design notes, with before and after rewrites.

title: Tamper detection and security requirements for an energy meter
summary: Turning the threats an electricity meter faces, from opened covers and magnets to neutral tricks, forged data and malicious firmware, into testable requirements for detection, data integrity, secure boot and event logs.

title: SystemVerilog Assertions for beginners: immediate vs concurrent, and your first property
summary: Learn the difference between immediate and concurrent assertions, exactly which values a concurrent assertion samples on a clock edge, and how to write and read a property for a request/acknowledge handshake.

title: System architecture of a BMS for e-rickshaw batteries: sensing, balancing and protection
summary: How to partition a BMS for a small lithium traction pack into cell sensing, current and temperature measurement, balancing, layered protection, precharge and communication, and the trade-offs at each boundary.

title: Synchronous vs asynchronous reset, and why "assert async, release sync" wins
summary: Entering reset is easy; leaving it is a timing event. See why asynchronous reset release can break a design, and how a two-flop reset synchronizer makes it safe.

title: Switching into VLSI from software or another branch: what transfers and what to learn
summary: Moving into chip design from software, mechanical, civil or another branch. Which of your skills carry over, which fundamentals you must rebuild, and one project that shows a reviewer the switch is real.

title: Switching between two clocks without a glitch
summary: A plain mux between two clocks can emit a runt pulse when its select changes. See how the cross-coupled glitch-free clock mux used for low-power modes works, and the assumptions it quietly relies on.

title: Superloop or RTOS? Deciding with timing requirements, not fashion
summary: A superloop with interrupts is enough more often than people think. Work out the worst-case loop time against each deadline, and you will see exactly which requirement, if any, calls for a preemptive scheduler.

title: Starting a chip-design startup: the first technical decisions
summary: The first technical decisions a chip startup makes, choosing the first product, the process node, which IP to build or license, the tool flow and a tape-out path, and how each one constrains the others and the budget.

title: Sourcing components for a hardware startup: from prototypes to production
summary: How sourcing changes from prototype to production: authorised channels, lifecycle status, lead times and reorder points, tested alternates, counterfeit risk and design choices that make a BOM buildable.

title: Skilling paths into embedded systems in India: from college lab to product team
summary: A project ladder that takes you from blinking an LED to firmware a product team would accept, with what each rung teaches and how to show it, from register-level drivers to an RTOS, tests and field updates.

title: Skilling paths into chip design in India: degrees, short programs and self-study
summary: What a degree, a short training program and self-study each give you on the way into chip design, what an employer can actually check, and how open-source projects tie the three together into evidence.

title: Six-step BLDC commutation in firmware: Hall sensors, PWM and timing
summary: How firmware turns three Hall sensor signals into the six switch patterns that spin a brushless DC motor, how to change PWM outputs without shoot-through, how to compute speed, and how to detect a stall.

title: Simulating an analog block across corners and with Monte Carlo
summary: One typical simulation proves little. Learn what process corners and Monte Carlo each model, script a PVT sweep around ngspice, and read a Monte Carlo spread as margin and confidence rather than one number.

title: Sigma-delta ADCs: trading speed for resolution with oversampling and noise shaping
summary: A one-bit quantizer inside a feedback loop, run far faster than the signal, plus a digital filter, gives high resolution at low bandwidth. See why noise shaping works, simulate it, and learn its limits.

title: Setup and hold time, explained with one flip-flop and a clock edge
summary: A flip-flop needs its input to sit still for a short window around the clock edge. Here is what that window is, why missing it breaks a design, and how to work out the fastest safe clock by hand.

title: Setting, clearing and testing register bits safely in C
summary: Masks and shifts for single bits and multi-bit fields, why read-modify-write can silently undo another write, and how set/clear registers and write-1-to-clear flags change the code you should write.

title: Setting up a hardware regression in CI: seeds, triage and flaky tests
summary: Structure a hardware regression as fast per-commit smoke runs and broad nightly random runs, record every seed, group failures by signature, and treat a flaky simulation as a bug in its own right.

title: Setting up a college VLSI lab on open-source EDA tools
summary: How to set up a college VLSI lab that runs on open-source tools, with suitable machines, a containerised and version-pinned toolchain, open PDKs and lab exercises that need no licence server.

title: Sequencing an ADC array from RTL: sample scheduling, channel muxing and buffering
summary: A sensor-fusion controller needs many channels sampled at known instants. Design the digital sequencer that schedules several multiplexed ADCs, respects settling time, timestamps each sample and buffers the results.

title: Sensor fusion basics: complementary and Kalman filters for orientation
summary: A gyroscope drifts and an accelerometer is noisy, but together they give a stable tilt estimate. How a complementary filter and a two-state Kalman filter combine them, with C and Python you can test.

title: Scoreboards and reference models: checking outputs you did not predict by hand
summary: Pair a Python reference model with a scoreboard so random tests check themselves. Covers in-order matching with a queue, out-of-order matching by tag, and the end-of-test checks that stop silent passes.

title: Scan chains and ATPG: how chips are tested after manufacturing
summary: Every manufactured chip must be tested for defects in seconds. Learn how scan turns flip-flops into a shift register, how ATPG generates patterns, and what fault coverage really measures.

title: Satellite navigation for timing: how receivers discipline clocks for grids and networks
summary: How a timing receiver uses satellite time to steer a local oscillator, why the loop trades short-term and long-term stability, what happens in holdover when signals are lost, and why grids and networks depend on it.

title: Sampling and aliasing: why an anti-alias filter comes before every ADC
summary: Sampling folds every frequency above half the sample rate back into the band you care about, where no software can remove it. See how folding works, compute where a tone lands, and size a simple filter.

title: Safety analysis for a drone controller: failure modes and fail-safe behaviour
summary: What a multirotor flight controller should do when it loses the control link, its position fix, a sensor or its supply, how to rank simultaneous failures, and why a reset in flight is a hazard in its own right.

title: Rural IoT node trade-offs: range, battery life, cost and maintenance
summary: How radio choice, reporting interval, battery and enclosure decisions pull against each other in a sensor node for farms and villages, with a battery-life model that shows which decisions matter most.

title: Running firmware without a board: QEMU and Renode in CI
summary: Emulators let every commit boot the real firmware binary, run its self-tests and check its output. How to make firmware report pass or fail to the emulator, script the run, and know what still needs hardware.

title: Running a trade study: criteria, weights and honest scoring
summary: A weighted trade study picks between architectures with criteria and weights agreed before scoring, a sensitivity check on the weights, and a written rationale that says what would change the answer.

title: Running a model with TensorFlow Lite Micro: the interpreter, arena and operators
summary: What happens between handing TensorFlow Lite Micro a model array and getting scores back - how it reads the model in place, plans memory in the arena, calls kernels, and how to link only the operators you use.

title: Running a field pilot for sensing hardware: from a handful of prototypes to real users
summary: How to plan a field pilot for sensing hardware, choosing sites, working through local partners, logging and updating devices remotely, planning maintenance visits and deciding up front what the pilot must prove.

title: Running a coverage review: which holes to close and which to waive
summary: How to triage coverage holes into missing stimulus, unreachable cases and spec questions, write waivers that a reviewer can check, and decide with evidence when a block's verification is done.

title: Routing and the DRC violations it leaves behind
summary: Global routing plans the paths, detailed routing draws the metal, and sometimes a few spacing, short or via violations remain. Learn what each kind means and how to clear it without breaking timing.

title: Ripple-carry vs carry-lookahead: where the delay goes in an adder
summary: An adder's delay is the time for a carry to travel. See why ripple-carry grows linearly with width, how generate and propagate signals let lookahead and prefix adders grow logarithmically, and when ripple is still right.

title: Reliability basics: failure rates, MTBF and the bathtub curve
summary: What a failure rate and MTBF actually say, why an MTBF of centuries does not mean a product lasts centuries, how early failures and wear-out differ, and how derating parts keeps the failure rate low.

title: Reading and citing standards: IS, IEC and IEEE documents for engineers
summary: How standards are numbered, revised and adopted across national and international bodies, how to read one without getting lost, and how to cite one so a reader can find exactly the document you used.

title: Reading a technical paper efficiently in three passes
summary: Read a technical paper in three passes, skim for the claim, read for the method, then check the evidence and what is left out, so you spend deep reading time only on papers that earn it.

title: Reading a spec like a bug hunter: looking for what it does not say
summary: Many hardware bugs start as gaps in the specification. Learn a repeatable way to read a spec for ambiguities, unstated corner cases and missing error behaviour, using a short watchdog timer description as the example.

title: Reading a public procurement specification as an engineer
summary: How to read a public tender's technical specification, turning it into testable requirements, a list of referenced standards, an acceptance test plan and a compliance matrix, and what to ask before bidding.

title: Reading a microcontroller datasheet and reference manual efficiently
summary: A microcontroller's documents run to thousands of pages. Which document answers which question, the order to read the sections in, and how a two-minute baud-rate check against the clock tree saves a day of debugging.

title: Reading a linker script: sections, memory regions and the map file
summary: How a GNU linker script places code and data in flash and RAM, why .data has two addresses, and how to use the map file, size and nm to find out what is eating your memory.

title: Reading a CMOS inverter's transfer curve: noise margins and switching point
summary: The voltage transfer curve of a CMOS inverter shows where it switches and how much noise it tolerates. Learn to read the switching point and noise margins, and how transistor sizing moves them.

title: Race conditions in firmware: shared variables between interrupts and tasks
summary: Why a 64-bit tick counter read on a 32-bit core can jump 49 days into the future, how read-modify-write loses updates, and the critical sections, retry loops and atomics that make shared data safe.

title: RV32I in one sitting: every instruction format and why it is laid out that way
summary: RV32I packs every instruction into one of six 32-bit formats. See each format field by field, decode real instructions by hand, and learn why fixed register positions keep the decoder small.

title: RTL to GDS in one page: what each step of the flow takes in and hands out
summary: The RTL-to-GDS flow is a chain of steps, each reading files and writing files you can open. Learn what goes in and comes out of synthesis, floorplan, placement, clock tree, routing and sign-off.

title: RISC-V traps and CSRs: what happens between an interrupt and your handler
summary: Follow a machine-mode trap step by step through mtvec, mepc, mcause and mstatus, write a minimal trap entry in assembly and C, and see exactly how mret puts everything back.

title: Python for hardware engineers: the parts you will use every day
summary: Hardware engineers use Python to parse tool reports, generate test vectors, plot results and write small reference models. Here are the parts of the language that matter, with working examples.

title: Putting analog and digital on one die: substrate noise, supplies and isolation
summary: Switching logic injects noise into the shared substrate, supplies and package that sensitive analog circuits sit on. Learn the coupling paths, and how guard rings, separate supplies and floorplanning keep them quiet.

title: Pruning and weight compression for tiny models
summary: Zeroing small weights only saves memory and time if the storage format and the hardware can exploit it. Unstructured versus structured pruning, index overhead, weight clustering, and checking what accuracy you gave up.

title: Proving a FIFO never overflows with SymbiYosys
summary: Write assertions, a reset assumption and covers for a small FIFO, run a SymbiYosys proof, and read the counterexample trace step by step when an undersized counter breaks the full flag.

title: Prototyping a small ML accelerator on an FPGA
summary: Build a MAC-lane array with on-chip buffers, attach it to a soft RISC-V core as a memory-mapped peripheral, and measure real end-to-end throughput with cycle counters, which is where the data-movement surprises appear.

title: Production test strategy: what to test on every unit and what to sample
summary: How to decide which tests every board gets, which are sampled, and where calibration fits, using fault coverage, escape rates and the rising cost of finding a fault later in the chain.

title: Priority inversion, and how priority inheritance fixes it
summary: A high-priority task waiting on a mutex held by a low-priority task can be delayed without bound by medium-priority work. A millisecond-by-millisecond timeline shows how it happens and how priority inheritance bounds it.

title: Presenting your project in a short technical talk
summary: Build a short project talk around one message and a problem-approach-result arc, with diagrams readable from the back row and a rehearsed demo that has a recorded fallback.

title: Preparing for experienced verification interviews: methodology questions and how to answer them
summary: Experienced verification interviews probe judgement, not syntax. Learn to explain your test plans, coverage decisions and debugging stories with concrete evidence from your own work.

title: Preparing for embedded interviews: C, interrupts and debugging stories
summary: Embedded interviews test pointers, bit manipulation, interrupt design and how you debug. Here is how to prepare each area, with worked questions and a structure for telling a bug story clearly.

title: Preparing for digital design interviews: the topics that recur and how to practise
summary: Digital design interviews keep returning to timing, FSMs, clock domain crossing, FIFOs and Verilog. Here is what each topic tests and how to practise by drawing, explaining and coding aloud.

title: Power cuts, surges and voltage swings: designing electronics for real-world grids
summary: How to design electronics that survive power cuts, surges and wide voltage swings, using brown-out detection with hysteresis, layered surge protection, wide-input supplies and a hold-up budget for saving state.

title: Post-training quantization vs quantization-aware training
summary: Post-training quantization calibrates a finished model; quantization-aware training simulates int8 while the model learns. How each works, how to diagnose the gap, and when the cheaper one is enough.

title: Portable Stimulus in plain terms: one test intent, many platforms
summary: Portable Stimulus describes what a test scenario must achieve as an abstract model, and lets a tool generate concrete tests for block simulation, SoC simulation and silicon. Here is the idea, with a small Python sketch.

title: Planning compliance testing early: EMC, safety and environmental tests
summary: Which kinds of compliance tests electronic products typically face, how to run cheap pre-compliance checks on the bench, and the design habits that give a product a good chance of passing the first time.

title: Placement and congestion: reading the heat map before routing fails
summary: Global placement spreads cells, legalisation and detailed placement make them fit, and the congestion map predicts whether routing will succeed. Learn to read that map and relieve hot spots early.

title: Pipelining a datapath step by step: latency, throughput and the cost of registers
summary: Cut a multiply-accumulate path into balanced stages, see how the clock period, latency and register count change, and carry a valid bit alongside the data so the pipeline knows which results are real.

title: Physical design for multiple voltage domains: level shifters, isolation and floorplan
summary: An always-on domain plus a switchable one needs separate power grids, power switches, isolation and level-shifter cells at the right boundaries. How to floorplan and place them, with a switch-sizing calculation.

title: Partitioning a NavIC receiver SoC between hardware correlators and firmware
summary: Count the operations in acquisition, tracking, data decoding and position solution for a NavIC receiver, and see why correlators belong in hardware while loop filters and navigation run comfortably in firmware.

title: Parasitic extraction and sign-off timing: why post-route numbers change
summary: Before routing, wire delay is a guess. After routing, extraction measures real resistance, capacitance and coupling. See with a worked RC example why a path that passed after placement can fail at sign-off.

title: Packaging basics: wire bond, flip chip and where chiplets fit
summary: A die is useless until a package connects it to a board, protects it and removes its heat. Learn how wire bonding and flip chip work, what package parasitics do, and why systems increasingly split into chiplets.

title: Open shuttles and shared tape-outs: how students can get a design onto real silicon
summary: How multi-project shuttles split the cost of a tape-out, what open PDKs and open-source flows make possible for students, and a practical checklist for preparing a small design for a shared run.

title: Op-amp stability and phase margin without the heavy maths
summary: Why an op-amp in feedback can ring or oscillate, explained with poles, loop gain and a Bode plot. Learn to read phase margin, why unity gain is the hardest case, and how compensation trades speed for stability.

title: On-device signal classification for a health wearable: possibilities and limits
summary: Small on-device models can flag patterns in body signals for follow-up, but a flag is not a diagnosis. Signal quality gates, the base-rate problem in numbers, and how to validate a wearable classifier responsibly.

title: Neural networks for hardware engineers: layers as multiply-accumulates
summary: A dense neural network layer is a matrix-vector product. Counting its multiply-accumulates, weights and activations tells you how much compute, flash and RAM the hardware must provide.

title: Moving ADC samples with DMA and double buffering
summary: Let DMA fill a circular buffer from the ADC while the CPU processes the half that is already full. How half-transfer and transfer-complete interrupts divide the work, how to budget time, and how to detect an overrun.

title: Moore or Mealy? Choosing an FSM style by timing, not by textbook
summary: A 101 sequence detector written as Moore and as Mealy shows the real difference: when the output appears, whether it can glitch, and how a registered output gives you the best of both.

title: Model-based systems engineering without the jargon
summary: Model-based systems engineering keeps what a system must do, how it is split up and how the parts connect in one linked model instead of scattered documents. Here is the idea in plain words, with an example.

title: Metal fill, density rules and why the fab cares about empty space
summary: Chemical-mechanical polishing needs even metal density, so empty regions get filled with dummy shapes. Learn how density windows are checked, how fill is inserted, and how its capacitance affects sign-off timing.

title: Memory ordering and FENCE: why a store may not be visible yet
summary: Write buffers and relaxed ordering let a RISC-V core make memory operations visible out of program order. See where that breaks device drivers and multi-hart code, and which FENCE fixes each case.

title: Memory BIST and JTAG boundary scan: testing what scan cannot reach
summary: Scan chains test logic but not memory arrays or the solder joints on a board. Learn how on-chip memory BIST runs march algorithms, and how JTAG boundary scan tests board interconnect through four pins.

title: Measuring model accuracy honestly: test sets, leakage and confusion matrices
summary: One accuracy number can hide a model that misses the class you care about. How to keep test data truly separate, spot leakage, and report per-class results from a confusion matrix.

title: Measuring cell voltages in a battery pack: the analog front end of a BMS
summary: Each cell in a series battery stack sits at a different, often high, common-mode voltage. Learn why simple dividers fail, how level shifting and stacked monitors measure each cell, and what balancing demands.

title: Making decisions on a soil sensor node: thresholds, rules or a model?
summary: Start a sensor node's decision logic with a threshold and hysteresis, add readable rules as needs appear, and bring in a model only when logged data shows the simple logic failing, using a soil moisture node.

title: Making a physical design flow reproducible: pinned tools, configs and seeds
summary: A layout result is only useful if someone else can produce it again. Learn how to pin the flow and PDK versions, keep configuration in version control, record seeds and write a run record anyone can follow.

title: Machine, supervisor and user mode: why RISC-V has privilege levels
summary: What machine, supervisor and user mode may each do, which kinds of systems need which combination, and how traps, delegation and the return instructions move execution between them.

title: MAC units and systolic arrays: how ML accelerators reuse data
summary: A systolic array is a grid of multiply-accumulate cells that pass operands to their neighbours, so each value fetched from memory feeds a whole row or column. The PE in Verilog, the skew, and a cycle count.

title: Low-power verification basics: what UPF adds to simulation
summary: Power intent adds domains that switch off, isolation at their boundaries and retention of state. Learn how power-aware simulation corrupts powered-down logic, and the sequencing bugs that only this reveals.

title: Low-power firmware: sleep modes, wake sources and measuring the current you saved
summary: How to choose a sleep depth from wake-up time and retained state, how to enter sleep without missing a wake-up, and how to measure average current properly instead of trusting a datasheet number.

title: Low-dropout regulators inside chips: the loop, stability and dropout
summary: An LDO is an op-amp driving a large pass transistor inside a feedback loop. Learn where dropout comes from, why the output pole moves with load current, and how the capacitor choice decides stability.

title: Lint warnings that point at real RTL bugs
summary: Width mismatches, multiple drivers, combinational loops and unused signals are the lint warnings most worth reading. Here is what each one usually means in real RTL, with examples and fixes.

title: Layering a testbench: stimulus, driver, monitor and checker
summary: Split a testbench into what to send, how to send it, what was observed and whether it was right. A plain cocotb example shows why this layering pays off even without a methodology library.

title: Latency budgets: splitting end-to-end response time across subsystems
summary: A user-visible deadline becomes a set of allowances for sensing, sampling, filtering, processing and actuation that each owner can design to and test, with the worst case, not the average, adding up.

title: Keeping interrupt handlers short: what belongs in an ISR and what does not
summary: A good interrupt handler acknowledges the hardware, captures the data that would otherwise be lost, and defers everything else. Here is why, with the arithmetic and the patterns for deferring work.

title: Keeping an AI log: recording what you asked, what you kept and why
summary: An AI log is a short record of each prompt, what came back, what you checked and what you kept. It makes AI use reviewable, shows you where the tool helps, and gives you honest answers in an interview.

title: Kconfig in Zephyr: turning features on without editing source
summary: How Zephyr's Kconfig decides what gets compiled, how prj.conf and menuconfig set options, why an option you set can silently stay off, and how to check what actually ended up in your build.

title: Jitter and phase noise: what they are and why ADCs and radios care
summary: Jitter is clock timing error seen in the time domain; phase noise is the same error seen in frequency. Learn the jitter definitions, convert a phase-noise plot to RMS jitter, and see how jitter caps ADC resolution.

title: Is your testbench any good? Checking it by injecting bugs on purpose
summary: Mutation testing seeds small deliberate faults into the RTL and checks that some test fails for each one. Learn the common mutation operators, how to read survivors, and a small Python script to run it.

title: Interrupt controllers in RISC-V SoCs: what the core-local and platform-level units do
summary: Timer and software interrupts stay local to each hart; external interrupts pass through a platform-level controller with priorities, thresholds and claim/complete. How the pieces fit and where they bite.

title: Interfacing pH, conductivity and turbidity sensors: the analog side
summary: Three common water-quality sensors need three different front ends. Learn why a pH electrode needs a near-zero-bias buffer, why conductivity uses AC excitation, and how turbidity sensing rejects ambient light.

title: Interface control documents: agreeing on the boundary before building
summary: An interface control document writes down the signals, protocol, timing, connectors and ownership at a boundary between two teams, so each can build its side in parallel and integration holds no surprises.

title: Int8 quantization explained: scale, zero point and what you lose
summary: How real-valued weights and activations are mapped to 8-bit integers with a scale and a zero point, how symmetric and asymmetric schemes differ, and where the accuracy actually goes.

title: Inside an asynchronous FIFO: why the pointers cross in Gray code
summary: An async FIFO works because each pointer crosses the clock boundary in Gray code, where only one bit changes per step. Learn the synchronization, the full and empty compares, and why the flags are safely pessimistic.

title: Inside a standard-cell library: Liberty, LEF and what the numbers mean
summary: A cell library is several files that describe the same cells for different tools. Learn what Liberty timing tables and LEF footprints contain, what drive strengths mean, and how a tool looks up one delay.

title: Inside a PLL: phase detector, charge pump, loop filter and VCO
summary: A phase-locked loop multiplies a slow, accurate crystal into a fast clock. Walk through what each block does, why the loop filter needs a resistor, and watch a simple model lock in Python.

title: Implementing activation functions in fixed point: ReLU, sigmoid and lookup tables
summary: ReLU is an exact clamp, any function of an int8 input is an exact 256-entry table, and wider inputs need interpolation. How to build each in fixed point and size its error against the output step.

title: Image preprocessing in hardware: downscaling, normalisation and windowing
summary: A streaming pixel pipeline crops, downscales and normalises camera data for a small network without ever storing a frame. Line buffers, a verified 2x2 downscaler in Verilog, and the rounding details that matter.

title: IR drop and electromigration in plain terms
summary: IR drop is supply voltage lost in the power grid, which slows cells today. Electromigration is metal worn away by current density, which breaks wires years later. Both are checked before tape-out.

title: How to run a design review, and how to take part in one
summary: Prepare the review package, run a short checklist-driven meeting, record every finding with a severity and an owner, and give and take feedback on the design rather than on the person.

title: How to read the RISC-V specification without getting lost
summary: A reading order for the RISC-V manuals, how extension names like RV32IMAC_Zicsr are built, how to read the encoding tables, and the handful of specification words that change what you must implement.

title: How to read a static timing report line by line
summary: A timing report is two sums, one for when data arrives and one for when it is needed. Walk through a setup path line by line and learn what launch, capture, arrival, required time and slack mean.

title: How smart energy meters work and why utilities deploy them
summary: How a smart meter measures energy from voltage and current samples, stores readings, talks to the utility and detects tampering, with a short Python example that computes real power the way a metering chip does.

title: How over-constrained assumptions make formal proofs lie
summary: An assumption that is too strong can make a formal proof pass while checking nothing. Learn how vacuous passes and conflicting assumptions arise, and how cover statements and assumption reviews expose them.

title: How deep should a FIFO be? Sizing it from burst length and rate mismatch
summary: A FIFO only has to hold the backlog that builds up while a burst arrives faster than it drains. Work out that backlog for a sensor burst, add margin for synchronizer latency, and check the idle-time condition.

title: How big should the stack be? Measuring and guarding stack use
summary: Stack overflow on a microcontroller corrupts data silently. Combine stack painting, the compiler's per-function stack reports and a guard region that faults on overflow to size stacks with evidence instead of hope.

title: How a chip goes from idea to market, step by step, from an Indian team's point of view
summary: The stages a chip passes through, from specification and design to fabrication, test, qualification and the product approvals that follow, and the decision each stage exists to make.

title: How a bandgap reference makes a voltage that ignores temperature
summary: A bandgap reference adds a base-emitter voltage that falls with temperature to a scaled thermal voltage that rises, so the sum stays flat. Work through the numbers, the circuit and what limits its accuracy.

title: How a SAR ADC converts: binary search with a capacitor DAC
summary: A successive-approximation ADC finds a digital code by binary search, one comparator decision per bit. Follow the sample, compare and bit-trial sequence, and see why the capacitor array sets the accuracy.

title: How a CMOS wafer is made: the fabrication steps every designer should picture
summary: Every layer you draw in a layout becomes a mask and a set of process steps. Follow a CMOS wafer from bare silicon through lithography, implant, etch, deposition and metallisation, mapped to the layers in a layout.

title: Harvard vs von Neumann in microcontrollers today
summary: Textbooks present Harvard and von Neumann as rivals. Real microcontrollers use separate instruction and data paths for speed and one shared address space for flexibility. Here is why both ideas survive.

title: Hardware/software co-design: deciding what to accelerate
summary: Profile the software first, use Amdahl's law to bound the gain, then move a hot loop into hardware only when the cost of starting it and moving its data is small next to the work it saves.

title: Hardening your first block with LibreLane: a guided first run
summary: Take a small registered design from Verilog to GDS with LibreLane on sky130. Write a minimal configuration, run the flow, and learn which reports and views to open first and what to look for in each.

title: Hand calculation before simulation: the analog designer's habit
summary: A simulator always gives an answer, right or wrong. Learn to estimate bias, gain and bandwidth on paper first, with a worked common-source example, so you can tell at a glance when a simulation result cannot be true.

title: Giving and receiving code review without bruised egos
summary: Code review goes well when changes are small, comments are specific, reviewers ask questions instead of issuing verdicts, and authors respond to every point. Practical habits for both sides of a pull request.

title: Git for hardware engineers: branches, reviews and generated files
summary: How to branch for RTL and firmware work, what belongs in the repository and what does not, how to handle large tool outputs, and how to review a hardware change so it lands safely on main.

title: Getting the most out of a mentor: bring questions, show work
summary: A mentor's time is limited, so the value comes from your preparation. Bring specific questions, share work in progress early, and act on feedback between meetings so each session starts further ahead.

title: Getting the most from hardware hackathons and design contests
summary: How to scope a hardware hackathon project small enough to finish, prepare parts and toolchains before the clock starts, divide work across a team and document what you built so it keeps paying off afterwards.

title: Gesture recognition from an IMU: data, features and a small model
summary: From recording wrist or handheld gestures to running a classifier on a microcontroller - defining classes, windowing six-axis motion data, compact features, a tiny network and the streaming loop on the device.

title: Functional coverage: deciding what to measure before you measure it
summary: Build a coverage model from verification plan items into coverpoints, bins and crosses for a small timer, and see why writing that model is really a design review of the specification.

title: From student to engineer: habits that matter in your first year at work
summary: The first year at work rewards habits more than brilliance. Keep a work notebook, write decisions down, raise problems early, finish small tasks completely and learn the codebase on purpose.

title: From single-cycle to a five-stage pipeline: what changes and why
summary: Cutting a single-cycle core into five stages adds pipeline registers, raises the clock and creates hazards. Work out the real speed-up, what each register must carry, and what new logic you inherit.

title: From schematic to Gerbers: designing a first board in KiCad
summary: The full path of a first circuit board in KiCad, using a small 3.3 V regulator board as the example, from symbols and footprints through layout and rule checks to the Gerber and drill files a fabricator needs.

title: From board to FPGA to chip: when a product earns a custom chip
summary: How one-time engineering cost, unit cost, volume, power, size and risk decide whether a function should stay on a board, move into an FPGA or become a custom chip, with a break-even calculation and its caveats.

title: Floorplanning decisions that make or break a block
summary: Aspect ratio, utilisation, macro placement and pin order are set in minutes at the floorplan and paid for hours later. Learn how each choice shows up as congestion or timing, with a worked sizing example.

title: Floorplanning a low-power drone controller chip: motor PWM, sensors and always-on logic
summary: A flight controller chip mixes noisy motor outputs, sensitive sensor interfaces, a processor and always-on logic. Work through partitioning it into regions, power domains and pin groups, and why each choice is made.

title: Fixed-point filters on a microcontroller without an FPU
summary: A second-order IIR filter in integer C with Q15 samples and Q14 coefficients, checked bit-exactly against a Python model, plus the accumulator, rounding and limit-cycle problems that floating point hides.

title: Fixed-point arithmetic for RTL designers: Q formats, rounding and saturation
summary: Convert a filter coefficient to Q1.15, track how bits grow through a multiply and an accumulate, and choose between truncation, rounding and saturation when you shrink the result back down.

title: Five assertion patterns that catch real bugs early
summary: One-hot state, stable-until-accepted, no overflow, eventual response and no X on outputs. For each pattern, the SVA you write, the bug it catches and the mistake that makes it useless.

title: Five SystemVerilog design features worth using from day one
summary: logic, always_ff and always_comb, enums, structs with packages, and unique case each turn a class of silent RTL bug into a tool error or warning. Here is what each one catches.

title: Firmware architecture for a smart energy meter: metering, events and logs
summary: How to structure smart meter firmware so metering is never disturbed by communication, tamper events are recorded reliably, and energy totals survive sudden power loss, with the hold-up and flash-wear arithmetic.

title: Finding the cause of a firmware crash from the trap state
summary: When a RISC-V core traps, three registers say what went wrong and where. Capture them with the stack pointer and return address, then walk the stack back by reading function prologues, as in this real QEMU example.

title: Finding and joining the open-source hardware community from India
summary: Where open-source hardware communities gather, from forums and repositories to meet-ups and shared tape-out groups, and how to make your first contributions genuinely useful to the people who maintain the projects.

title: Fabless, foundry, OSAT: who does what in the semiconductor chain
summary: The roles of chip design companies, wafer foundries, assembly and test houses, and EDA and IP providers, what each one hands to the next, and why the handoff files matter as much as the work.

title: FPGA prototyping as a verification step: what it finds that simulation misses
summary: Running RTL on an FPGA gives you long runs, real interfaces and real software, at the cost of visibility and fidelity. Learn which bugs prototyping finds, what it cannot tell you, and how to debug on the board.

title: FMEA step by step: severity, occurrence, detection and what to do next
summary: A walk through a failure mode and effects analysis on a water pump controller, from listing failure modes and rating them to turning the top risks into design changes and tests, then re-scoring.

title: Estimating hardware work: ranges, assumptions and the cone of uncertainty
summary: Why a single-number estimate for hardware work is almost always late, how to give ranges with stated assumptions, how a short simulation shows the real odds, and how estimates should narrow as the design matures.

title: Estimating chip area before you write RTL
summary: Count flip-flops, adders, multiplexers and memories, convert to gate equivalents, apply a utilisation, and you have an area estimate before any RTL exists. Then check it against your first synthesis run.

title: Equivalence checking: proving synthesis did not change your design
summary: How combinational and sequential equivalence checking compare a netlist with its RTL, what compare points and miters are, and why retimed flops, re-encoded state machines and X assignments need help.

title: Energy per inference: why memory access dominates
summary: Fetching an operand usually costs more energy than multiplying it, and the gap grows with distance. A simple energy model, worked for a dense and a convolution layer, shows why designers fight to keep data close.

title: Electronics for farms: sensing, connectivity and power in rural deployments
summary: The building blocks of a farm sensor node, from soil and weather sensors to long-range low-power radio and solar and battery power, with a worked energy budget and the maintenance realities that shape design.

title: Edge or cloud inference? Latency, power, privacy and cost
summary: Whether a model runs on the device or on a server is decided by a handful of questions about latency, connectivity, energy, privacy, cost and updates. Here they are, worked through for sensing products.

title: Edge AI for Indian languages: keyword spotting across languages and accents
summary: How to build an on-device keyword spotter that works across Indian languages and dialects, from consent-based data collection and small multilingual models to evaluation that reports the worst group, not the average.

title: ESD protection on chip pins: why every pad has diodes
summary: A touch from a charged hand can put amperes into a pin and kilovolts across oxide that fails at a few volts. Learn what ESD does to a chip, and how pad diodes and rail clamps steer the current safely away.

title: EMC basics for board designers: loops, return paths and edges
summary: Why edge rate, not clock frequency, sets how high a board's emissions reach, why every signal's return path must stay unbroken, and why filtering belongs at the connectors where cables become antennas.

title: Drone electronics for agriculture and mapping: what the controller must handle
summary: What a drone's flight controller must do for spraying and mapping work, from fast attitude control and navigation to payload control and failsafes, and why drone rules shape the electronics from the start.

title: Draw the circuit before you write the Verilog: the habit that prevents most RTL bugs
summary: Sketch the registers, muxes and logic first, write code that matches the drawing line for line, then check the code with AI and the tools. A moving-average filter shows the whole loop.

title: Directed tests or constrained random? Using each where it pays off
summary: Directed tests pin down the corners you know about; constrained random stimulus explores the ones you did not imagine. Learn when to use each, how to bias random towards corners, and why seeds matter.

title: Detecting machine anomalies from vibration on a microcontroller
summary: Spectral band energies, a baseline learned from normal running and a simple distance score catch many machine faults on a microcontroller. Build that first, then decide whether a neural network adds anything.

title: Designing low-cost health devices responsibly: accuracy, safety and approvals
summary: Why medical devices are regulated, how to validate a device's accuracy honestly against a reference with a Bland-Altman analysis, and how to avoid claims that a low-cost device cannot support.

title: Designing for dust, heat and moisture: environmental requirements for Indian conditions
summary: How to write environmental requirements for products deployed in hot, dusty, humid and monsoon-affected sites, and how they drive enclosure ratings, venting, coatings, part choices and tests.

title: Designing for a shared-shuttle tile: the area, I/O and clock limits that shape your RTL
summary: A small fixed tile on a shared chip limits your area, pin count and clock speed. Learn how those limits change RTL choices, with an area budget worked by hand, and what such a tape-out teaches and what it does not.

title: Designing an SoC memory map: regions, alignment and room to grow
summary: Lay out a small RISC-V SoC's memory map by hand, choose sizes and alignments that make address decoding cheap, make the holes fault instead of alias, and leave space for the next chip.

title: Designing a water quality monitoring system end to end
summary: A water quality monitor is sensors, calibration, enclosure, power, connectivity and maintenance working as one system. How to write requirements that tie them together, with a pH calibration worked through in code.

title: Designing a skid buffer to break a ready path without losing throughput
summary: A skid buffer registers the ready signal of a valid/ready interface and adds one spare slot to catch the word already in flight. Here is the design, traced cycle by cycle through a stall.

title: Designing a power grid: rings, straps and why IR drop starts at the floorplan
summary: Rings, straps and rails carry supply current from the pads to every cell. Learn how the grid is laid out, why its resistance sets the IR drop, and why it is far easier to plan early than to repair after routing.

title: Designing a memory-mapped register block that firmware engineers will thank you for
summary: A register block is the contract between hardware and firmware. Choose access types deliberately, define reset values, avoid read side effects, get write-one-to-clear right, and document it all from one source.

title: Designing a centre-aligned PWM block with dead time for a BLDC controller
summary: Build a centre-aligned PWM from an up/down counter, insert dead time so the high and low switches of a half-bridge are never on together, and update the duty cycle without glitches.

title: Designing a biopotential front end for a health wearable: gain, CMRR and input protection
summary: Body signals are millivolts riding on large electrode offsets and mains interference. See how input impedance, CMRR, a driven reference and staged gain recover them, and how input protection keeps the wearer safe.

title: Design for manufacture: small PCB decisions that change yield
summary: Footprints, part spacing, thermal balance, panelisation, fiducials and test points are small layout choices that decide whether an assembly line builds your board cleanly or produces rework.

title: Decoupling capacitors: why, how many and where to place them
summary: Chips draw current in short bursts that a distant regulator cannot supply. Local capacitors provide that charge, and a short calculation shows why their placement and loop area matter as much as their value.

title: Debugging bare-metal firmware with GDB and OpenOCD
summary: How GDB, OpenOCD and a JTAG probe fit together, and how to use breakpoints, watchpoints and memory examination to inspect a running microcontroller and its peripherals without adding a single printf.

title: Debugging as a career skill: hypotheses, experiments and notes
summary: Treat every bug as a small experiment: state a hypothesis, predict the result, change one thing, and record what happened in a debugging journal. The method works for RTL, firmware and boards alike.

title: Debugging an LVS mismatch without losing a day
summary: An LVS failure report can list hundreds of differences caused by one short. Learn a triage order for reading the comparison, isolating shorts and opens, and checking the usual suspects such as pins and well ties.

title: Debugging a failing test systematically: from the first mismatch to root cause
summary: A repeatable method for hardware test failures - reproduce, find the first divergence, narrow in time and hierarchy, and write down each hypothesis - with a script that finds where two traces first disagree.

title: Debouncing a push button in RTL, and why a counter beats a delay chain
summary: A mechanical button bounces for milliseconds when pressed. Learn why you synchronize the input first, how a small counter-based debouncer filters the bounce, and how to size the counter.

title: Data hazards and forwarding paths, traced cycle by cycle
summary: Trace read-after-write hazards on a five-stage pipeline diagram, see which bypass path covers each distance between producer and consumer, and write the forwarding unit with the right priority.

title: DRC, LVS and antenna checks: what each one protects you from
summary: Three checks stand between a layout and the fab. DRC asks whether it can be made, LVS whether it is the circuit you meant, and the antenna check whether manufacturing itself will damage your transistors.

title: DMA from the architecture side: bus masters, arbitration and coherence
summary: A DMA engine is a second bus master competing with the CPU. Work out arbitration latency and burst efficiency, and see why caches make DMA buffers tricky and what clean, invalidate and alignment fix.

title: Current mirrors: copying a current and why matching matters
summary: A current mirror copies one reference current to many places on a chip. Learn how the basic two-transistor mirror works, what its output resistance means, and how mismatch and channel-length modulation spoil the copy.

title: Crossing a multi-bit value between clock domains: handshake, mux recirculation or FIFO
summary: Synchronizing bus bits one by one can produce values that never existed. Compare the three safe structures for multi-bit crossings, what each assumes, what it costs, and how to choose.

title: Costing a bill of materials: what changes from prototype to volume
summary: Why the same board costs several times more as a prototype than in production, and how to build a cost roll-up that includes price breaks, attrition, setup charges, assembly, test and yield loss.

title: Convolution layer arithmetic: output size, MACs and memory by hand
summary: From kernel size, stride and padding to the output shape, then to multiply-accumulates, weights and activation bytes for one convolution layer, worked by hand and checked with a few lines of Python.

title: Contributing to open-source hardware and EDA projects
summary: How to make a first useful contribution to an open-source EDA tool or hardware project: pick a suitable issue, reproduce it, write a focused change with a test, and work with maintainers patiently.

title: Computing a CRC in hardware: from the polynomial to an LFSR and a parallel form
summary: Turn a CRC polynomial into a serial shift-register circuit, check it against a known test vector, then let a short script unroll it into XOR equations that process a whole byte per clock.

title: Comparators: speed, offset, hysteresis and kickback
summary: A comparator turns a tiny voltage difference into a clean digital decision. Compare static and latched designs, see where input offset and kickback come from, and size hysteresis that stops chattering.

title: Collecting your own sensor dataset: labels, balance and the boring parts that matter
summary: A small edge model is only as good as the data recorded with the real sensor. How to plan recordings, write a labelling guide, cover conditions, balance classes and document the dataset so it stays usable.

title: Clock tree synthesis: skew, latency and why zero skew is not the goal
summary: Clock tree synthesis balances arrival times across thousands of flops, but chasing zero skew wastes power and can hurt timing. Learn how latency and skew trade off and how useful skew fixes a critical path.

title: Clock gating without glitches: the latch-based integrated clock gate
summary: ANDing a clock with an enable can chop clock pulses and clock flops at the wrong time. See how a latch that is transparent while the clock is low keeps the gated clock clean, and how to use the cell properly.

title: Choosing an ADC architecture for a multi-channel sensor-fusion array
summary: When several sensors must be combined, when each channel is sampled matters as much as how well. Compare multiplexed and simultaneous sampling, resolution against speed, and area and power per channel.

title: Choosing a specialisation after a few years: depth, breadth or both
summary: After a few years in chips or embedded work you must decide whether to go deep, go broad or combine the two. How to judge which skills are scarce, when depth pays, and why adjacent knowledge makes you more effective.

title: Career paths in embedded systems: firmware, drivers, board support and test
summary: What application firmware, device driver, board support and embedded test engineers work on, the tools each one uses every day, and how people move from one role to another as their skills grow.

title: Career paths in chip design: what each role does day to day
summary: Front-end design, verification, physical design, DFT, analog, CAD and post-silicon validation, described by the work each role actually does in a normal week, the tools it lives in and the skills it rewards.

title: Caches from scratch: a direct-mapped cache worked by hand
summary: Split an address into tag, index and offset, then trace hits and misses for a short program in a tiny direct-mapped cache. One shifted array turns a 0% hit rate into 75%.

title: Cache coherence in two cores: the problem MESI solves
summary: Two cores with private caches can hold different values for one address. Trace a shared counter through the four MESI states on a snooping bus, and see why coherence alone does not make the increment atomic.

title: Building your own 12-week learning plan for VLSI or embedded
summary: A self-study plan works when it starts from a target role, sequences fundamentals before labs and labs before a project, and checks progress every week. How to build one for VLSI or embedded.

title: Building the pad ring: I/O cells, power pads and padframe planning
summary: The pad ring connects the core to the package and protects it from the outside world. Learn how to choose pad order and power pad count, what bonding constrains, and how the ring meets the core grid.

title: Building the energy accumulator of a smart meter in fixed-point RTL
summary: Multiply voltage and current samples, accumulate the products without overflow, and emit one calibrated pulse per fixed quantum of energy. A worked sizing of every register, checked with a Python model.

title: Building an engineering portfolio on GitHub that reviewers will read
summary: A reviewer gives your profile a few minutes. Show fewer, finished projects, each with a clear README, tests that pass, checked results and an honest note on which parts you did yourself.

title: Building a single-cycle RISC-V datapath on paper first
summary: Before writing CPU RTL, trace each instruction class through fetch, decode, execute, memory and write-back on paper. You get the control table, the muxes and the critical path almost for free.

title: Budgets as a design tool: allocating mass, cost and margin across subsystems
summary: A technical budget splits one system limit, such as mass or unit cost, into allowances for each subsystem, compares them with bottom-up estimates and holds back margin for the surprises every project has.

title: Branch prediction from static rules to two-bit counters
summary: Every wrong branch guess throws away pipeline work. Work out the cost of a misprediction, compare static rules with one-bit and two-bit predictors by hand, and see where each one fails.

title: Bounded proof or full proof? Model-checking depth and k-induction explained
summary: Why a bounded model check can pass while the induction step fails on a correct design, how unreachable states cause it, and when to raise k versus write an invariant that makes the unbounded proof go through.

title: Bootloaders and safe firmware updates: A/B slots, verification and rollback
summary: A firmware update must survive power loss at any instant and a new image that boots but misbehaves. How A/B slots, signed images, a trial boot and a confirm step give you that, and where designs usually go wrong.
